notes.title: Aging Farming Population
notes.rawContent:
Japan's agricultural workforce 
is **rapidly aging**.

Many farmers are already **over 65 years old**, 
creating labour shortages and 
increasing the **need for technologies** 
that improve productivity and accessibility.

---
### Why is Smart Agriculture important in Japan?

> **"One of the biggest challenges is that fewer young people are entering agriculture while the farming population continues to age.**
> 
> Smart agriculture isn't about replacing farmers. It's about helping them work more efficiently and making agriculture **more accessible for future generations**."

## References 

#### (1)

Research Nester, “Controlled environment agriculture market
size, share & trends analysis report,” 2025. [Online]. Available:

notes.title: Blackout Phase
notes.rawContent:
For a few days that I have not planted any Microgreens. 
There has been kind of a "Blackout" phase for a few weeks. 

Eating without the touch of Microgreens feels like an empty void. 
Before going back to growing some more seeds, let's break down one of the coolest concepts during the growth phase. The **Blackout**. 

> Concept: **Blackout**
> Growth phase where Microgreens start "reaching" for light. 
> When seeds sense no light, they start freaking out and cry for survival. 

In total darkness, microgreens seeds do not produce **clorophylle** (the green pigment). 
This is totally fine. 

But in this state, they are freaking out. 
And for this reason, they start the process of **etiolation**.

It is basically a survival instinct saying: *"Hey, either we get some light or we die."*.
So they start growing **taller**, **thinner** and **uniformly** for that quality look at the end, before the light hits. 

We are kind of "tricking" the plant making it think we are underground. Controlling its evolution in a precise way. Guiding it to full potential. 

### ⏱️ How long to blackout?

Usually **1 to 3 days**, depending on:

- Seed type
- Growth rate
- Desired height and look

Too long = weak, leggy greens.  
Too short = stunted growth.


---

notes.title: Coco coir soil
notes.rawContent:
Coco coir es básicamente la reutilización de 
residuos de coco para crear soil. 
Es biodegradable y perfecto para Microgreens. 

Dado que los nutrientes para los microgreens solo 
provienen del mismo seed, el agua y la fotosintesis, 
el soil no es tan importante. 
Esto es gracias a la **endosperm reserves**. 
En la primera fase, no se necesita soil para los nutrientes. 
El soil es simplemente un **anchor y delivery system** para el agua. 

Gracias a la capacidad de aireado del coco coir, (**macropores**) 
el oxigeno puede pasar perfectamente entre los seeds, 
y crear el ecosistema perfecto para que las microgreens crezcan. 

El Coco Coir genera canales de aire que se quedan abiertos, 
incluso cuando el medio está saturado de seeds o elementos. 

Tiene una buena capacidad de absorción y retención de agua. 
La humedad necesaria es perfecta para ellas. 

## 🔗 Sources 

- [Coco coir for microcreens](https://www.botanicoir.com/products/coconut-coir-microgreens/) 
- [What is coco coir](https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/garden-how-to/soil-fertilizers/planting-in-coco-peat-media.htm) 
- [Types and Conditions](https://greenplanetnutrients.com/blog/tips-advice/what-is-coco-coir/)

notes.rawContent:
## Micro-Universe

A Controlled-environment Agriculture (CEA) is like building 
an optimised micro-universe where conditions are created 
using technology, for life to evolve at its maximum potential. 

Inside this micro-universe, we really do not care about outside conditions, 
whether they are affected by Climate change, global warming, 
water shortages or natural disasters. 

## Pregunta

> What exactly is CEA?

> [!info] Definition
> Controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) -- which includes Indoor Agriculture (IA) and Vertical Farming -- consists of **crop production systems** in greenhouses or other structures that use horticulture and **engineering technique**s beyond conventional soil-based outdoor production. [[#(1)]]

## The Goal of CEA 

The goal of CEA is to **build stronger protection** from the outdoor environment while providing the **optimal conditions** of the crops using [[Precision Agriculture]] or other innovations. 

Achieving **long-term** [[Food Security]] and environmental sustainability by reducing resources being used while also making the most out of the land. 

As many scientists are pointing toward Risks to Life on Land from Global Warning, where changes in temperature, precipitation, and seasonal timing will alter the geographic ranges of many types of plants and animals [[#(2)]] . 

> If warming is kept to 2°C, 18% of insects, 16% of plants, and 8% of vertebrate animals are projected to lose over half of their geographic range [[#(2)]]. 

## Energy-Intensive systems 

CEA may reduce agricultural water usage by between 53%³ and 98%⁴, and chemical usage by as much as 100%; while using less land to produce the same amount of food as
conventional farming [[#(3)]]. 

This is great news, but there is a catch. 

One of the main challenges from these systems, is that they are often **energy-intensive** and costly to set up. 

This research will also focus on how to make this system as sustainable and resource-efficient as possible. 

## Challenges 

1. Energy Intensive 
2. Cybersecurity Threats to the Digital Ecosystem
3. Initial Cost to Set up 
4. Technical Expertise to manage effectively

---
## CEA Classification

1. Formats 
	1. Greenhouse 
	2. Vertical Farm 
2. Systems 
	1. Hydroponics 
	2. Soil-based 
3. Enabling Technologies 
	1. Energy management 
	2. Crop Science 
	3. Temperature / Humidity Control 
	4. Automation & Precision

## References 

#### (1)
[Controlled-environment agriculture Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controlled-environment_agriculture)
#### (2) 
[Risks to Life on Land](https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/climate-change-impacts/predictions-future-global-climate)
#### (3)
[Controlled-environment for sustainable future](https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2025-01/controlled_environment_agriculture_for_sustainable_development.pdf)
#### (Others)
[Climate Change Impacts](https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/climate-change-impacts/predictions-future-global-climate)
Darlene Steward and Greg Avery, “[Controlled-Environment Agriculture and the Geography of Food, Energy and Water](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy23osti/82104.pdf)
[The Future of Farming](https://viemose-dgs.dk/controlled-environment-agriculture/)

## Definition

According to **food security** defined by FAO [[#(3)]], national food security implies that **a**
**country has sufficient food for everyone**. 

Being the Agriculture sector, the responsible for providing "*food for everyone*", it is of great importance to have in mind all the possible threats and conditions that could destabilise the system for this to happen. 

> A fundamental step toward addressing food insecurity is for policymakers to assess their country's [[Food self-sufficiency Ratio]]. [4]

As stated on this research from Li C [[#(1)]], *"ensuring food security requires not only addressing*
*the most fundamental and direct factors but also incorporating a broader range of indirect factors that may impact food security into the research."* That means not only taking into account climate change, economic security or social changes, but also [[Cybersecurity in CEA]] and Resource efficient systems for the [[Controlled Environment Agriculture]] to be much more sustainable in the long run. 

> [!info] Most vulnerable sector
> With the increasing intensity of climate change and the growing frequency of extreme
   weather events, agriculture is one of the sectors most vulnerable to disruptions [[#(2)]]

notes.title: Hydroponics
notes.rawContent:
> [!info] Definition
> Hydroponics is based on growing plants without fertiliser. It is a more efficient way to provide your plants with nutrients and water. 

Plants do not actually use soil. Soil is simply soil. 
It does not taste like anything. In fact, it tastes bad. 
Plants actually absorb food and water from the soil. 

In a hydroponic garden, plants are given a nutrient formula and a medium for root growth to allow for much more direct and easier assimilation of nutrients and water. 

> Hydroponics is about making life easier for plants. 

The term *‘hydroponics’* comes from the Greek ‘*hydros*’, meaning ‘water’, 
and ‘*ponos*’, meaning “work”, so it literally translates as *‘water work’*.

Hydroponics has been shown to be a viable method of growing vegetables (**tomatoes**, **cabbage**, **cucumbers**, and **peppers**) as well as ornamental plants like **herbs**, **roses**, **freesia**, and **foliage** plants.

### Sources

-  [Introduction to Hydroponics](https://www.hydrofarm.com/introduction-to-hydroponics) 
- [A brief introduction to Hydroponics - Agribusiness Education and Research International](https://agribusinessedu.com/a-brief-introduction-to-hydroponics/) 
- [Hydroponics for Beginners | Everything You Need to Know for Successful Hydroponic Growth - YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tWgDqBryR30)

notes.title: Microgreens
notes.description: Exploring microgreens through Senku's scientific lens — high nutrient density, rapid growth, and minimal resource usage.
notes.rawContent:
Microgreens are the young seedlings 
of edible vegetables and herbs, 
harvested just after the cotyledon leaves develop. 

They pack intense flavor, 
concentrated nutrients, 
and can be grown in small spaces with minimal equipment. 

They’re the perfect intersection of *fast results* 
and *nutritional powerhouse*, 
making them an ideal candidate for 
**urban** and **space-age** agriculture.

In Taoist terms, 
they're the embodiment of [[Wu wei]],
minimal action, maximal return. 

## Microgreens Growth Process 

1. Seed selection 
2. Soaking 
3. Tray Setup 
4. Germination Phase 
5. Blackout Phase 
6. Light Phase 
7. Watering 
8. Harvesting

notes.title: Resource Efficiency

backlinks.context: In Precision Agriculture, one of the main goals is to reduce the use of resources such as water, light or energy (see Resource Efficiency.
backlinks.hoverContext: In Precision Agriculture, one of the main goals is to reduce the use of resources such as water, light or energy (see Resource Efficiency. With Resource-Constrained Systems, we try to accomplish the same goal but on the technological layer.

notes.rawContent:
Resource efficiency means 
**producing more food while 
using fewer natural resources**. 

Rather than maximizing production, the goal is 
to **reduce unnecessary** consumption of water, energy, fertilizer, 
and space **without compromising** crop quality.

---

For this objective, [[Precision Agriculture]] is used in [[Controlled Environment Agriculture]] along with [[Resource-Constrained Systems]]. Although this remains to be properly investigated. 

Hence, the resources needed to ensure [[Food Security]] are less, so that [[Long term Thinking]] is in mind for the future and reduce food imports. 

---
### Possible Question

> What resources are you trying to optimize?

> **"I'm mainly focusing on four resources: water, energy, fertilizer, and space.**
> 
> Small improvements in how we use these resources can have a significant impact, especially in small-scale indoor agriculture. My goal isn't simply to automate the system, but to make every resource work more efficiently."

## References 

#### (1)

Research Nester, “Controlled environment agriculture market
size, share & trends analysis report,” 2025. [Online]. Available:

notes.title: ATS
notes.description: AI Resume Scanners destroying applications just by parsing keywords.
notes.rawContent:
## Core Concept

Automated systems scanning résumés for keywords, structure, 
and signal quality—filtering which candidates even reach human orbit.

> [!info] Definition
> An applicant tracking system (ATS) is software that manages the recruiting and hiring process, including job postings and job applications. It organizes information about job seekers and makes it searchable. As its name implies, an ATS tracks candidates through the hiring process.
> Source: [Tech Target](https://www.techtarget.com/searchhrsoftware/definition/applicant-tracking-system-ATS)

## Problem Statement

Launch attempt #27:   
Another job-application torpedo fired into the void. No echo. No impact.   
Just cold digital space.  

Something’s off with the CV Document I'm using.   
Either patch the hull… or scrap it and build a new ship from raw ore.  

Leaning toward the second.   
Time to study the asteroid-sized gatekeeper: **ATS**.  

## Thinking Like ATS

Following the principle of Thinking Like Java,   
I should slip into the viewpoint of the ATS itself.   
Each keyword is a data packet.    
If the system is tuning for a specific harmony,   
my CV needs to resonate on the same frequency band. 

I used the *Teal Job Tracker App* to craft a cleaner, machine-friendly version.  
Stripped the noise. Boosted the signal.

<Cards> 
<Card href="https://www.tealhq.com/tools/job-tracker" title="Teal Job Tracker" > Fantastic Tool for Job Tracking and ATS Resume Builder </Card> 
</Cards>

## Key Takeaways

1. **Plain text over logos or images.**  
   Fancy visuals are just debris to an ATS scanner.
2. Emphasize **concrete achievements.**  
   Numbers > adjectives.
3. Stick to standard typography like **Arial**.  
   Readability = survivability.
4. Keep it a **one-pager.**  
   If a human gets the file, don’t bore them to death.

After the refit, deployed a few applications.  
Engines humming again. Systems online.

notes.rawContent:
## What is an Attack Surface?

An organization’s attack surface is the sum of vulnerabilities, pathways, or methods—sometimes called attack vectors—that hackers can use to gain unauthorized access to the network or sensitive data, or to carry out a cyberattack [[#(1)]]. 

It is the main factor to take in mind when talking about [[Cybersecurity in CEA]]. 

Since [[Precision Agriculture]] is mostly filled with digital assets, the new ecosystem provides a huge set of opportunities for Hackers to deliver a wide range of possible attacks. 

---
## Possible sub-surfaces

1. Digital attacks 
2. Physical attacks 
3. Social Engineering 

## References 

#### (1) 

IBM. *What is an attack surface?* 
Available at: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/attack-surface

notes.rawContent:
## Little academic attention

[[Controlled Environment Agriculture]] depend greatly of IoT systems for using [[Precision Agriculture]] to understand, manage, monitor and react to plant growth. 

As described in this research paper from Vakhnovskyi, A. [[#(1)]] , Modern CEA platforms integrate these three distinct technologies: 

1. **Field layer of Sensors**: Main IoT system of communication connected directly with the crops and using protocols like MQTT, Modbus or analog 4-20 mA. 
2. **Edge Computing layer**: Hosting real-time control logic from hardware gadgets such as Raspberry Pi or other microcontrollers. 
3. **Cloud layer**: Providing crop management, cross-facility transfer and persisting all necessary information about the whole system and authentication. 

This three layer architecture provides a huge [[Attack Surface]] that spans over the whole Information Technology domain. 

> Despite the critical role of CEA in food security, the cybersecurity of these systems has received remarkably little academic attention.
   Vakhnovskyi, A. [[#(1)]] 

Another report states that ransomware in Agriculture is easier because of the legacy systems that are being used [[#(2)]]. This is why investing in teaching and promoting a conscious Cybersecurity and Threat Model for small-scale businesses is key to provide more food security.

> [!warning] Rising Threats to Agriculture sector
> Ransomware attacks on the food and agriculture sector reached 265 incidents in 2025, more than doubling from 2023 [[#(2)]]

These findings seem to provide a clear idea on why investing in Cybersecurity for Agriculture plays a critical role on strengthening [[Food Security]] within the new era of farming. 

---

#### (1)
Vakhnovskyi, A. (2026). _Threat modeling and attack surface analysis of IoT-enabled controlled environment agriculture systems_. arXiv:2604.13308.
Available at: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.13308

Halcyon, “Ransomware attacks targeting agriculture and food production
doubled in 2025,” Halcyon Blog, 2025.
Available at: https://therecord.media/ransomware-attacks-food-and-ag-double-2025

notes.title: Food self-sufficiency Ratio
notes.description: The extent to which a country is able to meet its food needs with its own resources.

backlinks.context: A fundamental step toward addressing food insecurity is for policymakers to assess their country's Food self-sufficiency Ratio.
backlinks.hoverContext: A fundamental step toward addressing food insecurity is for policymakers to assess their country's Food self-sufficiency Ratio. [4]

notes.rawContent:
## Global Concern

Global [[Food Security]] is becoming an increasingly urgent concern. Despite differences in national contexts, countries worldwide share the goal of ensuring stable access to food[^1].

That means that we are all on the same page in regards to food production and accessibility. 

## Definition of FSSR

For improving the country's food self-sufficiency ratio, the expansion of *"domestic food production"* is needed. 

> [!info] Definition of FSSR by FAO
> The extent to which a country is able to meet its food needs with its own resources.

Due to the unstable political situation world-wide, the dependence on imported food may be aggravated in the future. 

That is why [[Fostering Public Understanding]] on how to become more self-sufficient, grow your own food and learning about smart agriculture techniques, will definitely improve this ratio. 

## How to calculate 

1. Covering both primary and secondary products 
2. Converting all food items into calories 
3. Calculating from the supply difficulties such as food losses or inventory rather than demand. 

## References 

[^1]: A new method for calculating the  FSSR[Online]. Available: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40066-025-00570-z

notes.title: Monozukuri
notes.rawContent:
Monozukuri literally means *"making things"*, 
but it also reflects a philosophy of **craftsmanship**, 
**continuous improvement** and **creating with care**.

It values **quality**, **precision** and [[Long term Thinking]] over quick results.

> **"During my visit to Japan I realized that people often approach their work with a level of care and attention that really resonated with me.**
> 
> Later I learned about the idea of _monozukuri_. I think that mindset fits very well with research, where progress often comes from continuous improvement rather than quick results."

notes.title: Shokuiku
notes.rawContent:
Shokuiku (食育) means **food education**.

It promotes a **deeper understanding** of food, 
nutrition, agriculture and where our meals come from (See [[itadakimasu]]).

The concept is officially supported by the Japanese government through the [[Basic Act on Food]] on Shokuiku.

---
### Why is food education important?

> **"I think technology should help people reconnect with food, not become more disconnected from it.**
> 
> That's why I really like the idea of _Shokuiku_. It reminds us that food isn't only something we consume—it's something we should understand and value. I think **technology can support that idea** rather than replace it."

notes.rawContent:
## The Language of Nature

Precision Agriculture is about understanding 
the language of nature. 

Each sensor is listening to the information that each plant 
or microorganism is saying. 

> [!info] Definition
> Precision agriculture comprises a set of technologies that combines sensors, information systems, enhanced machinery, and informed management to optimize production by accounting for variability and uncertainties within agricultural systems.
> Source: [Precision Agriculture and Food Security](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.1183899) 

Inside a [[Controlled Environment Agriculture]], Precision Agriculture helps to provide the necessary information to create the same optimal conditions for the plant to grow. 

> PA is conceptualized by a system approach to re-organize the total system of agriculture towards a low-input, high-efficiency, sustainable agriculture (Shibusawa, 1998)

---

- [PA Worldwide view](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0168169902000960)
- [Precision Agriculture Technology Book](https://books.google.de/books?hl=es&lr=&id=vHi9CgAAQBAJ&oi=fnd&pg=PP1&dq=Precision+agriculture&ots=4x3F2jfm_W&sig=dwI9lw1pK7nxschRjwj6y6xmwgE&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q=Precision%20agriculture&f=false)

notes.rawContent:
MQTT is one of the most 
widely used communication protocols for IoT.

It follows a **publish/subscribe** model 
and was specifically designed 
for devices with limited resources.

### Why MQTT?

> **"MQTT is lightweight and very efficient for small IoT devices.**
> 
> Since many agricultural sensors only send small amounts of data, MQTT allows them to communicate reliably while using very little bandwidth and energy. Since [[Edge Computing]] has some limitation, it fits perfectly for that."

notes.title: Resource-Constrained Systems
notes.description: Devices with strict limits on compute, memory, storage and energy.

backlinks.context: For this objective, Precision Agriculture is used in Controlled Environment Agriculture along with Resource-Constrained Systems.
backlinks.hoverContext: For this objective, Precision Agriculture is used in Controlled Environment Agriculture along with Resource-Constrained Systems. Although this remains to be properly investigated.

notes.rawContent:
A resource-constrained system is 
a device with **limited computing power, 
memory, energy, or storage**.

Examples include Raspberry Pi, 
ESP32 and many agricultural sensors.

Designing reliable software under these constraints is one of the main challenges of IoT engineering.

---
## Strict Limits

**Resource-Constrained Systems** are characterised by having strict limits on **compute**, **memory**, **storage** and **energy**, influencing design, development and deployment choices. 

These systems run on low resources, so they are more available, sustainable and maintainable, but do have some **security challenges** as well. 

In [[Precision Agriculture]], one of the main goals is to reduce the use of resources such as water, light or energy (see [[Resource Efficiency]]. With **Resource-Constrained Systems**, we try to accomplish the same goal but on the technological layer. 

> [!warning] Security Challenges
> Resource-constrained IoT devices face particular security challenges that originate from fundamental hardware limitations, trust management complexities, and systemic architectural vulnerabilities [[#(1)]]. 

Since **Resource-Constrained IoT Devices** need to take in mind the computational overhead, light-weight algorithms, criptography and systems need to be implemented from early development [[#(1)]].

Although deploying these kind of systems inside a [[Controlled Environment Agriculture]], may have real positive impacts, the [[Cybersecurity in CEA]] needs to be much more robust in these cases. 

> This resource-conscious approach ensures that these devices can fulfill their roles effectively without becoming a burden on resources or energy consumption. [[#(2)]]

## Common Constraints 

1. Complexity Challenge 
2. Memory Constraints 
3. Energy Efficiency Dilemma 
4. Network Limitations 
5. Security Considerations

## Problems inside IoT Devices 

1. Limited battery 
2. Small memory (RAM / Flash)
3. Low processing power

## Memory Optimisation Techniques 

- Buffering 
- Data compression 
- Efficient data structures 

---
## Benefits

As stated by [[#(2)]], these limitations are not drawbacks, but strategic choices that serve specific purposes. They are Design choices with multiple benefits such as:  

1. Efficiency and Energy Conservation 
2. Cost-Effectiveness 
3. Specialized Functionality 
4. Scalability 
5. Reduced Maintenance 
6. Low Network overhead

## References 

#### (1)

Neagu, M.; Serban, C.M.; Hangan, A.; Sebestyen, G. Trustworthiness in Resource-Constrained IoT: Review and Taxonomy of Privacy-Enhancing Technologies and Anomaly Detection. _Telecom_ **2026**, _7_, 10. https://doi.org/10.3390/telecom7010010

#### (2)

Medium, Poonam G, *Managing Resource-Constrained IoT Devices: Unlocking Potential Amidst Limitations*. https://medium.com/plexusbit-software/managing-resource-constrained-iot-devices-unlocking-potential-amidst-limitations-be932269e846

#### (3)

Youtube. Learn@Home. *Resource System Constraint Design*.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ngWnvUcFosY

#### (4)

Nawaz, Majid & Babar, Muhammad. (2025). IoT and AI for smart agriculture in resource-constrained environments: challenges, opportunities and solutions. Discover Internet of Things. 5. 10.1007/s43926-025-00119-3. 
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/389822619_IoT_and_AI_for_smart_agriculture_in_resource-constrained_environments_challenges_opportunities_and_solutions
